name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
overview: Adversaries subvert Kerberos authentication by stealing or forging tickets to enable Pass the Ticket. Kerberos realms involve three parties — a client, a service, and a Key Distribution Center (KDC) that issues the tickets after authentication. Depending on which credential material an adversary already holds (the krbtgt hash, a service account's hash, or simply the ability to make requests as an authenticated user), they can forge a ticket that impersonates any account, forge one scoped to a single service, brute-force a legitimately-issued ticket offline, or lift a ticket straight out of a running session's credential cache. Windows ships a built-in `klist` utility for listing and inspecting cached Kerberos tickets.

prerequisite_concepts.term: The three Kerberos actors and two ticket types
prerequisite_concepts.explanation: A client authenticates once to the KDC's Authentication Service (AS) and receives a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) — proof of domain authentication, encrypted with the krbtgt account's key. From then on, the client presents that TGT to the KDC's Ticket Granting Service (TGS) to request a service ticket (TGS) for whatever specific resource it wants to reach, and that service ticket is encrypted with the target SERVICE account's own key, not krbtgt's. This TGT-vs-TGS split is exactly why Golden Tickets (which need krbtgt's hash) and Silver Tickets (which need one service account's hash) are forged differently and have very different blast radii.

An SPN is what binds a Kerberos service ticket request to a specific service account — every service running under a domain account (SQL Server, IIS App Pool, etc.) registers one. By protocol design, any authenticated domain user can request a TGS ticket for any registered SPN, no special privilege required. That's not a bug — it's how Kerberos normally works — but it's also the entire precondition that makes Kerberoasting possible: an attacker just has to ask, then try to crack what comes back.

Kerberos tickets are encrypted with one of several negotiable algorithms. RC4-HMAC (etype 23 / 0x17) derives its key directly from the account's NTLM hash and is unsalted, which is exactly why an RC4-encrypted service ticket can be brute-forced offline straight back to a crackable hash. AES128/AES256 (etype 17/18) use a stronger, salted key derivation that resists this. A domain that has fully moved to AES-only Kerberos meaningfully raises the cost of both Kerberoasting and AS-REP Roasting — which is why 'unexpected RC4 in an AES-enforced environment' is one of the most reliable detection signals across this whole technique family.

Pre-authentication requires the client to encrypt a timestamp with its own key before the KDC will issue a TGT — proof the client actually knows the password, not just that it knows the username. It exists specifically to prevent an attacker from requesting AS-REP data for an arbitrary username and cracking it offline. Some accounts have it explicitly disabled (a legacy interoperability setting some applications historically needed), and that setting is the entire precondition for AS-REP Roasting.

T1558 sits one layer up the credential-material stack from T1003: a stolen NTLM/DCC2 hash (T1003) still has to be exchanged for a ticket at some point to reach a Kerberos-authenticated resource, whereas a stolen or forged ticket (T1558) skips that exchange entirely and can be replayed directly. That's also why several T1558 sub-techniques are direct payoffs of a T1003 dump — krbtgt's hash from T1003.003/T1003.006 becomes a Golden Ticket here.

prerequisite_concepts.term: Ticket lifetime as a forgery tell
prerequisite_concepts.explanation: A standard Active Directory domain's Default Domain Policy caps a TGT's lifetime at 10 hours ("Maximum lifetime for user ticket"). Forging tools default to far longer validity unless an operator deliberately overrides it — a multi-day or multi-year ticket lifetime on a 4769 event is one of the more reliable golden-ticket tells precisely because matching the legitimate default takes extra, easy-to-forget effort on the attacker's part.

subtechniques.name: Golden Ticket
subtechniques.overview: The krbtgt service account encrypts and signs every Kerberos TGT issued in a domain. An adversary who obtains krbtgt's password hash — typically via T1003.003 (NTDS) or T1003.006 (DCSync) — can forge a TGT for any account, with any group membership, entirely offline: a Golden Ticket. Because the KDC will accept any TGT it can correctly decrypt with krbtgt's key, a forged one is functionally indistinguishable from a real one to the domain controller unless its metadata gives it away.

concepts.term: Why this one credential unlocks the whole domain
concepts.explanation: Every TGT a real domain controller issues is encrypted and signed with krbtgt's key, and every domain controller trusts a TGT purely because it can decrypt and verify that signature — not because it remembers issuing it. That statelessness is intentional Kerberos design (it's what lets any DC in a domain validate tickets without querying every other DC), but it also means whoever holds krbtgt's hash can mint a TGT for an account that doesn't even exist, with Domain Admin membership baked in, without ever touching a domain controller to do it.

concepts.term: Why the forged ticket doesn't need a real AS-REQ
concepts.explanation: Normally a TGT only exists because a client sent an AS-REQ and the KDC's Authentication Service replied with an AS-REP. A Golden Ticket skips that exchange entirely — Mimikatz or Rubeus constructs the ticket structure locally and encrypts it with the stolen krbtgt key, then the attacker presents it straight to the TGS for a service ticket. The resulting absence of a matching 4768 before the 4769 is exactly the gap most Golden Ticket detections key on.

procedure_examples.activity: Used Mimikatz to generate Kerberos golden tickets.
Leverages its integrated Mimikatz implementation to obtain and use golden tickets.
Capable of forging ticket-granting tickets given krbtgt's key material.
Incorporates the Rubeus framework for golden ticket forgery.
kerberos::golden module builds and encrypts a forged TGT from a supplied krbtgt hash.

data_sources.detail: TGS request using a forged TGT — the tell is a 4769 with no corresponding legitimate 4768 for that logon session, or an RC4 (0x17) encryption type in an otherwise AES-enforced domain.
Absence of an expected AS-REQ (4768), or a ticket-renewal (4770) pattern inconsistent with the account's real logon history.
A validity period far exceeding the domain's configured Maximum Lifetime for User Ticket (default 10 hours) — forging tools default to much longer unless explicitly overridden.

detection_queries.title: TGS Request with No Preceding TGT (Possible Golden Ticket)
detection_queries.description: Flags 4769 service ticket requests for an account/session with no matching 4768 TGT request shortly before it — the classic Golden Ticket gap, since forged TGTs never go through a real AS-REQ.
detection_queries.query:
let TgtRequests = SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4768
| project TargetUserName, TgtTime = TimeGenerated;
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4769
| where ServiceName !endswith "$"
| join kind=leftanti TgtRequests on TargetUserName
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, TargetUserName, ServiceName, TicketEncryptionType, IpAddress
| order by TimeGenerated desc

detection_queries.title: Kerberos TGS Request with Anomalous RC4 Encryption
detection_queries.description: Flags RC4-encrypted service ticket requests in environments that should be AES-only — a common Golden/Silver Ticket tell since forged tickets from older tooling default to RC4.
detection_queries.query:
title: Kerberos Service Ticket Request with RC4 Encryption
id: 6c2d8f1a-3b7e-4a9c-9d2f-1e5a8c3b7f60
status: stable
author: H3AD-SEC Detection Engineering
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 4769
    TicketEncryptionType: '0x17'
  filter_machine_accounts:
    ServiceName|endswith: '$'
  condition: selection and not filter_machine_accounts
falsepositives:
  - Legacy applications or devices that only support RC4 and haven't been migrated to AES
level: medium
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1558.001

false_positives: Legacy applications, printers, or appliances that only support RC4 Kerberos encryption and haven't been migrated to AES
Monitoring gaps around DC restarts or log rotation can create apparent 4769-without-4768 gaps that are actually just missing telemetry, not a forged ticket
response_steps: Treat a confirmed Golden Ticket as full domain compromise — the krbtgt hash is out, and every account's trust boundary is void
Reset the krbtgt password twice, waiting for replication convergence between resets, to invalidate all existing golden tickets
Force a domain-wide credential reset and review Domain Admins/Enterprise Admins membership for anything added during the suspected window
Hunt for the original T1003.003/T1003.006 event that exposed krbtgt in the first place — the ticket forgery is the payoff, not the root cause

mitigations.name: Active Directory Configuration
mitigations.detail: Reset the krbtgt password twice to invalidate existing golden tickets; rotate it on a regular schedule (e.g. every 180 days).

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Restrict Domain Admin logons to domain controllers; delegate other admin functions to separate, lower-privilege accounts.

related.name: DCSync
related.relation: The usual source of the krbtgt hash a Golden Ticket needs — DCSync pulls it directly via replication, no code execution on a DC required.

related.name: NTDS
related.relation: The other common source of krbtgt's hash — extracted from ntds.dit itself rather than over the wire.

related.name: Silver Ticket
related.relation: The narrower sibling technique: scoped to one service's hash instead of krbtgt, trading blast radius for stealth since it never touches the KDC.

related.name: Pass the Ticket
related.relation: The forged TGT is only useful once it's actually injected into a session and used — that reuse step is Pass the Ticket.

subtechniques.name: Silver Ticket
subtechniques.overview: Where a Golden Ticket needs krbtgt's hash, a Silver Ticket only needs one service account's password hash (a SQL Server service account, a SharePoint app pool identity, or a machine account) — typically obtained via OS credential dumping or Kerberoasting. The forged TGS ticket is scoped to whatever that one service can do, which is more limited than a Golden Ticket, but the forgery never involves the KDC at all, so it leaves a much thinner audit trail on the domain controller.

concepts.term: Why it bypasses the KDC entirely
concepts.explanation: A legitimate TGS ticket is issued by the KDC's Ticket Granting Service after validating a presented TGT. A Silver Ticket skips that whole exchange: since the attacker already holds the target service account's key, they can encrypt a valid-looking service ticket themselves and hand it straight to the target service — the domain controller is never involved, so no 4768 or 4769 gets logged for that access at all.

concepts.term: Why detection has to move off the DC
concepts.explanation: Because there's no DC-side Kerberos event to catch, Silver Ticket detection has to rely on the target service's own logs (application audit logs, IIS/SQL logons) showing a Kerberos-authenticated session with no matching request on any domain controller in that same window — an absence-based correlation rather than a single matching event, which is inherently noisier and harder to automate than the Golden Ticket gap.

procedure_examples.activity: Forges Kerberos tickets using the AZUREADSSOACC account hash for hybrid-identity attacks.
Leverages its integrated Mimikatz implementation for silver ticket creation.
Generates silver tickets programmatically given a service account's key.
kerberos::golden module (with a service SPN specified) forges a silver ticket the same way it forges golden tickets.

data_sources.detail: A Kerberos-authenticated session or logon on the target service with no corresponding 4769 on any domain controller in the surrounding window.
Network logon (Type 3) via Kerberos on the service host itself, which is the only place this activity reliably surfaces.
PAC (Privilege Attribute Certificate) validation anomalies or a signature that doesn't match the expected KDC validation chain.

detection_queries.title: Kerberos-Authenticated Service Logon with No DC-Side Ticket Request
detection_queries.description: Correlates a service-side Kerberos logon against the absence of a matching TGS request on domain controllers — the practical Silver Ticket signal, at the cost of needing service-side telemetry alongside Security event logs.
detection_queries.query:
title: Kerberos Service Logon Without Corresponding TGS Request
id: 9a4e7c2d-5f1b-4d8a-9c3e-7b2f6a1d4c80
status: experimental
author: H3AD-SEC Detection Engineering
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 4624
    LogonType: 3
    AuthenticationPackageName: 'Kerberos'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - This selection alone is extremely broad; it must be correlated against an absence of matching 4769 events on the domain's DCs for the same account/service/time window before treating it as suspicious
level: low
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1558.002

false_positives: This technique is inherently hard to false-positive on directly since there's no single suspicious event — the risk is false negatives from incomplete service-side logging, not false alarms

Legitimate cross-forest or cross-domain Kerberos delegation scenarios can produce logon patterns that superficially resemble a missing-DC-event gap; validate against known delegation configurations first
response_steps: Identify which service account's hash was compromised — the ticket is only useful against that one service, so scope the response to it rather than the whole domain
Reset that service account's password (twice if it has delegation rights) and review its recent authentication history for anything else suspicious
Check how the hash was obtained in the first place (T1003 dump vs T1558.003 Kerberoasting) and close that root cause
Move the service account to a Group Managed Service Account (gMSA) where possible — its password is long, random, and rotated automatically, which sharply narrows this attack surface going forward

mitigations.name: Encrypt Sensitive Information
mitigations.detail: Deploy AES Kerberos encryption for service accounts instead of RC4.

mitigations.name: Password Policies
mitigations.detail: Enforce strong (25+ character) service account passwords with expiration, or use Group Managed Service Accounts.

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Restrict service account privileges and group memberships to the minimum the service actually needs.

related.name: Golden Ticket
related.relation: The broader sibling technique: forges against krbtgt instead of a single service, trading stealth for domain-wide reach.

related.name: Kerberoasting
related.relation: A common source of the service account hash a Silver Ticket needs, if the account wasn't already compromised via OS credential dumping.

related.name: Security Account Manager
related.relation: Another common source of a service account's hash when that account is also a local account on the host being targeted.

subtechniques.name: Kerberoasting
subtechniques.overview: Any authenticated domain user can request a TGS ticket for any registered Service Principal Name — that's normal Kerberos behavior, not a misconfiguration. When the returned ticket is RC4-encrypted, the encrypted portion is effectively the service account's NTLM hash used as a key, making it crackable offline with no further access to the network required. An attacker just requests tickets for every SPN they can enumerate, takes them offline, and lets a cracking rig grind against them.

concepts.term: Why any user can trigger this — it's not a permission bug
concepts.explanation: Kerberos is designed so that requesting a service ticket doesn't require any special right beyond being an authenticated domain user with a valid TGT — the KDC's job is to issue the ticket, not to decide whether you should be allowed to try authenticating to that service. Authorization happens later, at the service itself. That means Kerberoasting isn't exploiting a flaw; it's exploiting the fact that the request step and the authorization step are intentionally separate, and the request step alone hands you crackable material.

concepts.term: Why RC4 specifically is what makes it crackable
concepts.explanation: When a TGS ticket is encrypted with RC4-HMAC (etype 23), the encryption key used is derived directly from the service account's NT hash. Since RC4 in this construction is unsalted, an attacker can take the encrypted ticket data offline and try candidate passwords by deriving the same NT-hash-based key and checking whether decryption produces a well-formed ticket structure — exactly what tools like hashcat mode 13100 do. AES-encrypted tickets use a salted, far more expensive key derivation, which is why forcing AES-only Kerberos is the single most effective mitigation here rather than any detection rule.

concepts.term: Why the target is service accounts, not regular users
concepts.explanation: Only accounts with an SPN registered against them are kerberoastable — that's overwhelmingly service accounts (SQL, IIS, custom applications), because that's what SPNs exist for. Those accounts are also disproportionately likely to have old, never-rotated, weak, or shared passwords precisely because they're configured once during a deployment and rarely touched again — making them the softest targets even though the technique itself works against any SPN-bearing account.

procedure_examples.activity: Used Rubeus, Mimikatz's Kerberos module, and the Invoke-Kerberoast cmdlet to steal AES/RC4 service ticket hashes.
Obtained TGS tickets for Active Directory SPNs to crack offline.
Employed Invoke-Kerberoast PowerShell commands for credential access and lateral movement.
GetUserSPNs.py requests and formats service tickets for John the Ripper and Hashcat.
kerberoast module requests service tickets for every discoverable SPN and outputs crackable hashes.

data_sources.detail: TGS request with TicketEncryptionType 0x17 (RC4); the signal strengthens sharply when one account requests tickets for many distinct SPNs in a short window.
Execution of Rubeus, Invoke-Kerberoast, GetUserSPNs.py, or similar tooling, or PowerShell with kerberoast-related cmdlets on the command line.
A burst of LDAP queries enumerating accounts with a servicePrincipalName attribute set, the reconnaissance step that usually precedes the actual ticket requests.

detection_queries.title: Kerberoasting: Burst of RC4 TGS Requests Against Distinct SPNs
detection_queries.description: Flags accounts requesting an unusually high number of RC4-encrypted service tickets for distinct services in a short window — the volumetric Kerberoasting signature.
detection_queries.query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4769
| where TicketEncryptionType == "0x17"
| where ServiceName !endswith "$" and ServiceName != "krbtgt"
| summarize RequestCount = count(), DistinctSPNs = dcount(ServiceName) by TargetUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctSPNs >= 3
| order by DistinctSPNs desc

detection_queries.title: Kerberoasting Tool Execution (Cortex XDR)
detection_queries.description: Cortex XDR process-creation equivalent, catching the common Kerberoasting tooling by command-line pattern.
detection_queries.query:
dataset = xdr_data
| filter event_type = ENUM.PROCESS and event_sub_type = ENUM.PROCESS_START
| filter action_process_image_command_line contains "kerberoast" or action_process_image_command_line contains "GetUserSPNs"
| fields agent_hostname, actor_effective_username, action_process_image_command_line, event_timestamp

detection_queries.title: Kerberoasting via Invoke-Kerberoast / Rubeus / GetUserSPNs
detection_queries.description: Flags process execution of the most common Kerberoasting tooling by command-line pattern.
detection_queries.query:
title: Kerberoasting Tool Execution
id: 2e7c9b4a-6d3f-4a1e-8b7c-3f9a2d6e1b50
status: stable
author: H3AD-SEC Detection Engineering
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_rubeus:
    CommandLine|contains: 'kerberoast'
  selection_invoke:
    CommandLine|contains: 'Invoke-Kerberoast'
  selection_impacket:
    CommandLine|contains: 'GetUserSPNs'
  condition: 1 of selection_*
falsepositives:
  - Authorized red team or penetration testing activity
  - Security research in isolated lab environments
level: high
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1558.003

false_positives: Legitimate application startup or connection-pool recycling can request several service tickets in a short window; scope the rule to a meaningfully high distinct-SPN count, not just any burst
Vulnerability scanners and AD health-check tools that legitimately enumerate SPNs and request tickets as part of a security assessment
response_steps: Identify every SPN the account requested tickets for — each one is a service account whose password should be considered potentially exposed
Rotate the password for any targeted service account, prioritizing ones with weak/old passwords or broad privileges
Check for follow-on use of cracked credentials: new logons from those service accounts from unfamiliar hosts
Migrate targeted accounts to Group Managed Service Accounts where feasible to remove this attack surface long-term

mitigations.name: Encrypt Sensitive Information
mitigations.detail: Enable AES Kerberos encryption instead of RC4 wherever possible — this is the mitigation that actually breaks the offline-cracking path.

mitigations.name: Password Policies
mitigations.detail: Enforce 25+ character service account passwords with periodic rotation, or use Group Managed Service Accounts / password vaulting.

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Keep service accounts out of Domain Admins and limit their privileges to what the service actually needs.

related.name: AS-REP Roasting
related.relation: The sibling offline-cracking technique: same crackable-Kerberos-material idea, but targets accounts with pre-authentication disabled instead of SPN-bearing service accounts.

related.name: Silver Ticket
related.relation: A cracked service account hash from Kerberoasting is exactly the material a Silver Ticket needs to forge access to that same service.

related.name: Password Cracking
related.relation: The mandatory next step — the captured ticket is useless until the offline cracking actually recovers the password.

subtechniques.name: AS-REP Roasting
subtechniques.overview: Accounts configured with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled will respond to an AS-REQ from anyone claiming to be them, with no proof of password knowledge required. The AS-REP that comes back contains a portion encrypted with that account's key — if that key is RC4-derived, it's crackable offline exactly like a Kerberoasted ticket, except the attacker never needed valid credentials to trigger the request in the first place, only the target username.

concepts.term: What pre-authentication actually prevents, and why some accounts lack it
concepts.explanation: Standard Kerberos requires a client to encrypt a timestamp with its own key as proof of password knowledge before the KDC issues a TGT — without that, anyone could request AS-REP data for any username and try to crack it, since the KDC would produce a response regardless of whether the request came from the real account holder. Pre-authentication exists specifically to stop that. Some accounts still have it explicitly disabled, almost always for legacy application compatibility reasons predating wider Kerberos adoption, and that setting is the sole precondition this technique needs — no credentials, no network position beyond reaching a DC, just a valid username.

concepts.term: Why this is 'easier' than Kerberoasting but rarer to find
concepts.explanation: Kerberoasting requires being an authenticated domain user already, even an unprivileged one. AS-REP Roasting requires nothing but network line-of-sight to a domain controller and a list of usernames to try — no valid credentials at all. What limits its real-world impact is scope: only accounts with pre-auth explicitly disabled are vulnerable, and that's a much smaller, more unusual population than 'every service account with an SPN,' so the first step in practice is always enumerating which accounts even qualify before attempting the technique.

procedure_examples.activity: asreproast module reveals credentials of accounts that have Kerberos pre-authentication disabled.
Used AS-REP Roasting via Rubeus during intrusions documented October–November 2020.

data_sources.detail: AS-REQ / AS-REP exchange with Pre-Authentication Type 0 (or the field blank) — the direct signature of a pre-auth-disabled account being targeted.
Follow-on TGS activity from the account shortly after, if the cracked password is used to request further access.
Enumeration queries filtering for userAccountControl values with the DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH flag set — the reconnaissance step that identifies which accounts are even targetable.

detection_queries.title: AS-REQ Without Pre-Authentication (Possible AS-REP Roasting)
detection_queries.description: Flags 4768 events where Pre-Authentication Type is 0, the direct signal of a pre-auth-disabled account being queried.
detection_queries.query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4768
| where PreAuthType == "0" or isempty(PreAuthType)
| project TimeGenerated, TargetUserName, IpAddress, TicketEncryptionType, PreAuthType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

detection_queries.title: AS-REP Roasting via Rubeus (Cortex XDR)
detection_queries.description: Cortex XDR process-creation equivalent of the Rubeus asreproast detection.
detection_queries.query:
dataset = xdr_data
| filter event_type = ENUM.PROCESS and event_sub_type = ENUM.PROCESS_START
| filter action_process_image_command_line contains "asreproast"
| fields agent_hostname, actor_effective_username, action_process_image_command_line, event_timestamp

detection_queries.description: Flags execution of Rubeus's asreproast module by command-line pattern.
detection_queries.query:
title: AS-REP Roasting via Rubeus

subtechniques.name: Ccache Files
subtechniques.overview: On Linux and macOS, an authenticated Kerberos session's tickets live in a credential cache (ccache) file so the user isn't re-prompted for every service they touch. On Linux these are typically in /tmp, named krb5cc_<UID> or krb5.ccache; macOS keeps an equivalent in memory under an API:{uuid} scheme. An adversary who can read another user's ccache — usually as root, or via the same user context — can lift its tickets directly and reuse them (Pass the Ticket), or convert them to Windows format with tools like Kekeo for cross-platform lateral movement.

concepts.term: Why the credential cache exists at all
concepts.explanation: Kerberos's whole value proposition is single sign-on: authenticate once, then present tickets instead of a password for every subsequent service. The ccache file is simply where that session's tickets are held so `kinit` doesn't have to run again for each connection. It is functionally the Linux/macOS analogue of what the Windows LSASS process holds in memory for T1003.001 — a live session's usable credential material sitting in one place.

concepts.term: Why file permissions are the whole defense
concepts.explanation: A ccache file is normally readable only by the owning user (or root). There's no additional encryption protecting it at rest beyond standard filesystem permissions — so root access on a multi-user host, a misconfigured shared /tmp, or a privilege-escalation bug that grants read access to another user's files is sufficient to lift their live Kerberos session wholesale, no password or hash cracking required at all.

A ticket lifted from a Linux ccache is a standard Kerberos ticket — the protocol doesn't care what OS issued or is presenting it. Converting it to the format Windows tooling expects (what Kekeo is for) lets an attacker pivot a Linux-side credential theft straight into Windows-side lateral movement, which is why this sub-technique matters even in mixed environments where the initial foothold was Unix-based.

procedure_examples.activity: getST.py and ticketer.py can steal or forge Kerberos tickets using ccache files given a password, hash, aesKey, or TGT.

data_sources.detail: File read/copy access to /tmp/krb5cc_* or any path referenced by the KRB5CCNAME environment variable, by a process other than the owning user's normal session.
Execution of klist, kinit with an unusual KRB5CCNAME override, or ticket-conversion tooling like Kekeo.
Ticket reuse from a source context inconsistent with the original session (different host, different process tree) shortly after a ccache file was accessed.

detection_queries.title: Ccache File Access Rule
detection_queries.description: Base auditd watch for reads of the standard Linux ccache location and any KRB5CCNAME-overridden path.
detection_queries.query:
auditctl -w /tmp -p r -k ccache_access
auditctl -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S open,openat -F key=krb5cc -F path=/tmp

detection_queries.title: Non-Owner Access to Kerberos Ccache File
detection_queries.description: Flags a process reading a krb5cc_* file it does not own, the core signal for ccache theft on a shared host.
detection_queries.query:
title: Non-Owner Kerberos Ccache File Access

    file.path|contains: 'krb5cc_'
    file.action: 'read'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - System services (SSSD, cron under the owning user) that legitimately read their own session's ccache file — scope the rule to non-owner reads specifically
level: medium
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1558.005

false_positives: SSSD and other legitimate system Kerberos tooling routinely read ccache files as part of normal session management for the owning user
Backup or monitoring agents running as root that legitimately traverse /tmp as part of unrelated housekeeping
response_steps: Identify which user's session was compromised and every ticket that was live in that ccache at the time
Treat every service that session had active tickets for as potentially accessed by the attacker
Force re-authentication (kdestroy + kinit) for the affected user and rotate their password if the underlying access vector suggests broader compromise
If tickets were converted for cross-platform reuse (Kekeo), extend the hunt to Windows-side logon events for the same account

mitigations.name: Audit
mitigations.detail: Enable auditd scans of hash/ticket/tmp file access; disable Kerberos in sssd/Vintela configurations where it isn't actually needed.

mitigations.name: Credential Access Protection
mitigations.detail: Use SELinux to define entry points, process types, and file labels that restrict which processes can read ccache files.

related.name: LSASS Memory
related.relation: The closest Windows analogue: both target a live session's already-usable credential material sitting in one place, rather than a database that has to be decrypted first.

related.name: Pass the Ticket
related.relation: The direct next step once a ticket is lifted from the ccache — reusing it without re-authenticating.
